Local null-controllability of a system coupling Kuramoto-Sivashinsky-KdV and elliptic equationsThanks: ∗Institute of Mathematics, Czech Academy of Sciences, Žitná 25, Prague 1, Czech Republic, e-mail: bhandari@math.cas.cz (corresponding author)Thanks: †Indian Institute of Science Education and Research Kolkata, Campus road, Mohanpur, West Bengal 741246, India; e-mail: sm18rs016@iiserkol.ac.in

Kuntal Bhandari∗, and Subrata Majumdar†
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

This paper deals with the null-controllability of a system of mixed parabolic-elliptic pdes at any given time T>0T>0. More precisely, we consider the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky–Korteweg-de Vries equation coupled with a second order elliptic equation posed in the interval (0,1)(0,1). We first show that the linearized system is globally null-controllable by means of a localized interior control acting on either the KS-KdV or the elliptic equation. Using the Carleman approach, we provide the existence of a control with the explicit cost C​eC/TCe^{C/T} with some constant C>0C>0 independent in TT. Then, applying the source term method developed in [39], followed by the Banach fixed point theorem, we conclude the small-time local null-controllability result of the nonlinear systems.

Key words and phrases: 
KS-KdV-elliptic system, null-controllability, Carleman estimates, source term method, fixed point argument
2010 Mathematics Subject Classification
35M33, 93B05, 93B07, 93C20

1. Introduction and main results

1.1. Bibliographic comments and motivations

The controllability of coupled partial differential equations has gained immense interest to the control communities since the past few decades. Due to the significant importance of the parabolic models in physical, chemical and biological sciences, several methods have been developed to study their controllability properties. We first address the pioneer work by Fattorini and Russell [17, 18] where the authors utilized the spectral strategy, i.e., the so-called moments method to study the controllability (distributed or boundary) of 1D linear parabolic equations. Regarding the distributed controllability of parabolic pdes in dimension higher than 11, we refer the well-known Lebeau-Robbiano spectral method [38] (see also [36]) which is based on a global elliptic Carleman estimate. Next, we must mention that the global Carleman estimate, established by Fursikov and Imanuvilov in [25] has been intensively used to study the controllability of parabolic equations and systems. In this context, we refer the work [22] by E. Fernández-Cara and S. Guerrero where a global Carleman estimate has been established to study the controllability properties of some linear and certain semilinear parabolic equations. Later on, the controllability of a system of two parabolic equations with only one control force has been proved by S. Guerrero [28].

However, in most cases the Carleman approach is inefficient to handle the boundary controllability of the coupled parabolic systems. In fact, the boundary controllability for such systems is no longer equivalent with distributed controllability as it has been observed for instance in [21]. Due to this reason, most available results are in 1D and mainly based on the moments method. Among the fewest, we refer for instance, [1], [2], [3], [6]. For the multi-D situation, we address the work [5] where the boundary controllability results are obtained in the cylindrical geometries.

In the direction of controllability of nonlinear parabolic systems, we mention the work by E. Fernández-Cara and E. Zuazua [24] where the authors proved small-time global null-controllability of semilinear heat equations with the growth of nonlinear function |f⁡(r)|≤|r|​ln3/2⁡(1+|r|)|f(r)|\leq|r|\ln^{3/2}(1+|r|), see also [4] by V. Barbu. Very recently, the large-time global null-controllability of semilinear heat equations has been obtained in [35] for nonlinearities ff growing slower than |r|​ln2⁡(1+|r|)|r|\ln^{2}(1+|r|) under the sign condition: f⁡(r)>0f(r)>0 for r>0r>0 and f⁡(r)<0f(r)<0 for r<0r<0.

Another fascinating area in control theory is the study of controllability properties of the fourth order parabolic equation: ut+γ1​ux​x​x​x+γ2​ux​x+u​ux=0u_{t}+\gamma_{1}u_{xxxx}+\gamma_{2}u_{xx}+uu_{x}=0 (γ1,γ2>0\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2}>0), the so-called Kuramoto-Sivashinsky (KS) equation. This has been popularly studied in the past decades, such as [11], [44], [10], [42]. In particular, the authors in [10] proved that the linear KS equation with Neumann boundary conditions is null-controllable by a control acting in some open subset of the domain. The author in [42] proved the boundary local null-controllability of the KS equation by utilizing the source term method (see [39]) followed by the Banach fixed point argument where a suitable control cost C​eC/TCe^{C/T} of the linearized model plays the crucial role. Similar strategy has been applied in [31] to study the boundary local null-controllability of a simplified stabilized KS system (see below about this system). In this regard, we must mention that the nonlinearity u​uxuu_{x} in the KS system also appears in the Burgers equation: ut−ux​x+u​ux=0u_{t}-u_{xx}+uu_{x}=0, and concerning the controllability results of this equation we address the following works: [23], [27], [26].

To include dispersive and extra dissipative effects in the KS equation, a coupled system containing fourth (Kuramoto-Sivashinsky-Korteweg-de Vries, in short KS-KdV equation) and second order parabolic (heat) equations, under the name of stabilized Kuramoto-Sivashinsky system

(1.1) {ut+γ1​ux​x​x​x+ux​x​x+γ2​ux​x+u​ux=vx,vt−Γ​vx​x+c​vx=b​ux,\displaystyle\begin{cases}u_{t}+\gamma_{1}u_{xxxx}+u_{xxx}+\gamma_{2}u_{xx}+uu_{x}=v_{x},\\ v_{t}-\Gamma v_{xx}+cv_{x}=bu_{x},\end{cases}

has appeared for instance in [40]. The controllability of such system has been considered in several works, namely [9], [12], [13], [8], [33]. E. Cerpa, A. Mercado and A. F. Pazoto in [13] demonstrated the local null-controllability of (1.1) by means of localized interior control acting in the KS-KdV equation. Then, E. Cerpa along with N. Carreño [8] proved the local null-controllability to the trajectories with a localized interior control exerted in the heat equation. Two different types of Carleman estimates for the linearized model followed by the inverse mapping theorem have been implemented to conclude their controllability results. We also point out that recently, the controllability of KS-KdV-transport model has been discussed in [34]. Finally, it is worth mentioning that an insensitizing control problem for the stabilized KS system has been explored in [7].

Study of the parabolic-elliptic model, namely

(1.2) {ut−ux​x=a​u+b​v,−vx​x=c​u+d​v,\begin{cases}u_{t}-u_{xx}=au+bv,\\ -v_{xx}=cu+dv,\end{cases}

enlarges the literature of the control of pdes and such type of models significantly appear in several physical, chemical and biological situations: as for example, the prey-predator interaction, tumor growth therapy etc. One may refer to the works [20], [29], [30], [41] concerning the controllability issues of such systems.

In the work [20], the authors proved the local null-controllability of a semilinear parabolic-elliptic equation by means of a localized interior control acting in one of the two equations. Similar question has been addressed in [29] for the chemotaxis system of parabolic-elliptic type which is specially known as Keller-Segel model. Both papers utilized the Kakutani’s fixed-point theorem to handle the nonlinearity. In [41], a local interior null-controllability of such system with local and nonlocal nonliearity has been established using appropriate Carleman estimates and fixed point argument. The paper [19] dealt with the same issue for a system coupling two parabolic models and an elliptic model with one scalar control force, locally supported in space.

These works principally motivate us to study the null-controllability of a parabolic-elliptic system of coupled Kuramoto-Sivashinsky-Korteweg-de Vries equation and a second order elliptic equation. In fact, the coupled system of KS–elliptic equations can be seen as nonlocal KS equation. In this regard, we mention the work [32] where the author studied the analyticity properties of solutions of the nonlocal KS equations arising in the problem of a perfectly conducting thin-film flow down an inclined plane in the presence of an electric field. We also quote the work [16], where the dynamical behavior of some certain non-local KS system has been studied. However, we are mostly interested in the mathematical analysis from the view point of null-controllability of the mentioned systems by means of a single localized control.

1.2. The systems under study

Let T>0T>0 be any finite time and define QT:=(0,T)×(0,1)Q_{T}:=(0,T)\times(0,1). We also take any non-empty open set ω⊂(0,1)\omega\subset(0,1). Then, we consider the following control problems

(1.3) {ut+γ1​ux​x​x​x+ux​x​x+γ2​ux​x+u​ux=a​v+χω​h,in ​QT,−vx​x+c​v=b​u,in ​QT,\begin{cases}u_{t}+\gamma_{1}u_{xxxx}+u_{xxx}+\gamma_{2}u_{xx}+uu_{x}=av+\chi_{\omega}h,&\text{in }Q_{T},\\ -v_{xx}+cv=bu,&\text{in }Q_{T},\end{cases}

with the constants (a,b)∈ℝ2(a,b)\in\mathbb{R}^{2} such that b≠0b\neq 0; or

(1.4) {ut+γ1​ux​x​x​x+ux​x​x+γ2​ux​x+u​ux=a​v,in ​QT,−vx​x+c​v=b​u+χω​h,in ​QT,\begin{cases}u_{t}+\gamma_{1}u_{xxxx}+u_{xxx}+\gamma_{2}u_{xx}+uu_{x}=av,&\text{in }Q_{T},\\ -v_{xx}+cv=bu+\chi_{\omega}h,&\text{in }Q_{T},\end{cases}

with a≠0a\neq 0. Here hh is some control function (to be determined) localized in ω\omega, acting either through the KS-KdV equation or elliptic equation; γ1,γ2>0\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2}>0 denote the coefficients accounting the long wave instabilities and the short wave dissipation respectively. Finally, we consider the velocity c>−π2c>-\pi^{2}, the first eigenvalue of ∂x​x\partial_{xx} with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions, (one can find similar condition on cc in [20], [14]).

The boundary conditions for the state components are given by

(1.5) {u(t,0)=0,u(t,1)=0,t∈(0,T),ux(t,0)=0,ux(t,1)=0,t∈(0,T),v(t,0)=0,v(t,1)=0,t∈(0,T),\begin{cases}u(t,0)=0,\ u(t,1)=0,&t\in(0,T),\\ u_{x}(t,0)=0,\ u_{x}(t,1)=0,&t\in(0,T),\\ v(t,0)=0,\ v(t,1)=0,&t\in(0,T),\end{cases}

and the initial condition is

(1.6) u⁡(0,x)=u0​(x),x∈(0,1).u(0,x)=u_{0}(x),\quad x\in(0,1).

Looking into the coupled system (1.3) or (1.4), it is seen that we consider only one localized control function `​`​h​"``h" and to obtain the null-controllability for the linearized system, it is necessary to achieve a suitable observability inequality for the associated coupled adjoint system with single observation term (depending on which component we exert the control). To obtain this, we shall use the Carleman estimates for KS and elliptic equations and then remove the unusual observation terms with help of the coupling term(s). We shall observe this in Sections 3.1 and (4.1). Then, applying the source term method followed by a fixed point theorem (see [39]), we achieve the local controllability of the nonlinear systems.

We now prescribe the main results of our present work.

1.2.1. Controllability results of the nonlinear systems

Theorem 1.1 (Control on KS-KdV equation).

Let be (a,b)∈ℝ2(a,b)\in\mathbb{R}^{2} with b≠0b\neq 0. Then, the system (1.3)–(1.5)–(1.6) is small-time locally null-controllable around the equilibrium (0,0)(0,0), that is to say, for any given time T>0T>0, there is a R>0R>0 such that for chosen initial data u0∈H−1​(0,1)u_{0}\in H^{-1}(0,1) with ‖u0‖H−1​(0,1)≤R\|u_{0}\|_{H^{-1}(0,1)}\leq R, there exists a control h∈L2​((0,T)×ω)h\in L^{2}((0,T)\times\omega) such that the associated solution (u,v)(u,v) satisfies

(u⁡(T,x),v⁡(T,x))=(0,0),∀x∈(0,1).\left(u(T,x),\,v(T,x)\right)=(0,0),\quad\forall\,x\,\in(0,1).

Our next main result is the following: when a control force is acting only on the elliptic equation.

Theorem 1.2 (Control on elliptic equation).

Let be (a,b)∈ℝ2(a,b)\in\mathbb{R}^{2} with a≠0a\neq 0. Then, the system (1.4)–(1.5)–(1.6) is small-time locally null-controllable around the equilibrium (0,0)(0,0), that is, for any given time T>0T>0, there is a R>0R>0 such that for chosen initial data u0∈H−1​(0,1)u_{0}\in H^{-1}(0,1) with ‖u0‖H−1​(0,1)≤R\|u_{0}\|_{H^{-1}(0,1)}\leq R, there exists a control h∈L2​((0,T)×ω)h\in L^{2}((0,T)\times\omega) such that the associated solution (u,v)(u,v) satisfies

u⁡(T,x)=0,∀x∈(0,1),lim supt→T−‖v⁡(t,⋅)‖H−1​(0,1)=0.u(T,x)=0,\quad\forall\,x\,\in(0,1),\qquad\limsup_{t\to T^{-}}\|v(t,\cdot)\|_{H^{-1}(0,1)}=0.
Strategy of proofs
  • –

    First, we shall prove the global interior null-controllability results of the associated linear models, given by

    (1.7) {ut+γ1​ux​x​x​x+ux​x​x+γ2​ux​x=a​v+χω​h,in ​QT,−vx​x+c​v=b​u,in ​QT,\begin{cases}u_{t}+\gamma_{1}u_{xxxx}+u_{xxx}+\gamma_{2}u_{xx}=av+\chi_{\omega}h,&\text{in }Q_{T},\\ -v_{xx}+cv=bu,&\text{in }Q_{T},\end{cases}

    or,

    (1.8) {ut+γ1​ux​x​x​x+ux​x​x+γ2​ux​x=a​v,in ​QT,−vx​x+c​v=b​u+χω​h,in ​QT,\begin{cases}u_{t}+\gamma_{1}u_{xxxx}+u_{xxx}+\gamma_{2}u_{xx}=av,&\text{in }Q_{T},\\ -v_{xx}+cv=bu+\chi_{\omega}h,&\text{in }Q_{T},\end{cases}

    with the boundary and initial conditions as given by (1.5) and (1.6) respectively.

    The global Carleman estimate will help us to prove the null-controllability of the above linearized systems with a proper control cost C​eC/TCe^{C/T}. This is crucial to deduce the local controllability results for the non-linear models.

  • –

    Next, we shall apply the source term method introduced in [39]; more precisely, we prove the null-controllability of our linearized models with additional source term (in the KS equation) from some suitable Hilbert space which is exponentially decreasing while t→T−t\to T^{-}.

  • –

    After that, we use the Banach fixed-point argument to obtain the local null-controllability for the non-linear models.

1.2.2. Controllability results of the associated linearized systems

Theorem 1.3.

Let any u0∈H−2​(0,1)u_{0}\in H^{-2}(0,1) and T>0T>0 be given and (a,b)∈ℝ2(a,b)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}. Then, we have the following.

  1. (1)

    When b≠0b\neq 0, there exists a control h∈L2​((0,T)×ω)h\in L^{2}((0,T)\times\omega) such that the system (1.7)–(1.5)–(1.6) is null-controllable at time TT, that is,

    (u⁡(T,x),v⁡(T,x))=(0,0),∀x∈(0,1).\left(u(T,x),\,v(T,x)\right)=(0,0),\quad\forall\,x\in(0,1).
  2. (2)

    Similarly when a≠0a\neq 0, there exists a control h∈L2​((0,T)×ω)h\in L^{2}((0,T)\times\omega) such that the solution of (1.8)–(1.5)–(1.6) satisfies

    u⁡(T,x)=0,∀x∈(0,1),lim supt→T−‖v⁡(t,⋅)‖H−2​(0,1)=0.\displaystyle u(T,x)=0,\ \ \forall\,x\in(0,1),\qquad\limsup_{t\to T^{-}}\|v(t,\cdot)\|_{H^{-2}(0,1)}=0.

In both cases, the control function hh has the following estimate:

(1.9) ‖h‖L2​((0,T)×ω)≤C​eC/T​‖u0‖H−2​(0,1),\displaystyle\|h\|_{L^{2}((0,T)\times\omega)}\leq Ce^{C/T}\|u_{0}\|_{H^{-2}(0,1)},

where the constant C>0C>0 neither depends on TT nor on u0u_{0}.

Remark 1.4.

Note that, we need the initial data u0u_{0} to be at least in H−1​(0,1)H^{-1}(0,1) to study the null-controllability of the nonlinear systems whereas to study the linearized models, u0∈H−2​(0,1)u_{0}\in H^{-2}(0,1) is fine. The reason is that we need some more regularity of the set of solutions (u,v)(u,v) to conclude the required local controllability results for the systems (1.3) or (1.4); see Section 3.3.

Notations

Throughout the paper, CC denotes the generic positive constant which may depend on γ1,γ2\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2}, a,b,ca,b,c but does not depend on u0u_{0} or TT, and change from line to line.

We sometimes use the short notations Hm​(X)H^{m}(X) or 𝒞0​(X)\mathcal{C}^{0}(X) to denote the spaces Hm​(0,T,X)H^{m}(0,T;X) and 𝒞0​([0,T],X)\mathcal{C}^{0}([0,T];X) respectively, for some m∈ℤm\in\mathbb{Z} and XX is a Lebesgue space.

Paper organization

The paper is organized as follows:

  • –

    In Section 2, we just point out the well-posedness of the linearized control systems, which is more or less standard.

  • –

    Section 3 is devoted to study the null-controllability of our parabolic-elliptic model where a localized control is acting on the KS-KdV equation. Thereafter, in Section 4, we study the case when a control force acts in the elliptic equation only. In both cases, the controllability of the associated linearized models will be established by global Carleman estimates and then using the source term method followed by a fixed point argument, we shall study the nonlinear systems; see Section 3.3 for more details.

  • –

    Finally, we conclude our paper with some remarks and open questions related to the KS-KdV-elliptic system, given by Section 5.

2. Well-posedness of the linearized systems

This section is devoted to discuss the well-posedness of the linear systems (1.7)/(1.8)–(1.5)–(1.6). Let us first write the system (1.7) in infinite dimensional ODE setup:

where the operators 𝒜\mathcal{A}, ℬ\mathcal{B} are given by

and

D⁡(𝒜)={u∈H4​(0,1):u⁡(0)=u⁡(1)=ux​(0)=ux​(1)=0}.D(\mathcal{A})=\big\{u\in H^{4}(0,1):u(0)=u(1)=u_{x}(0)=u_{x}(1)=0\big\}.

ℬ∗​h​(t)=χω​h​(t,⋅).\mathcal{B}^{*}h(t)=\chi_{\omega}h(t,\cdot).

Therefore, one has the following adjoint system to (1.7)/(1.8)–(1.5)–(1.6), given by

(2.4) {−σt+γ1​σx​x​x​x−σx​x​x+γ2​σx​x=b​ψ+g,(t,x)∈QT,−ψx​x+c​ψ=a​σ,(t,x)∈QT,σ(t,0)=0,σ(t,1)=0,t∈(0,T),σx(t,0)=0,σx(t,1)=0,t∈(0,T),ψ(t,0)=0,ψ(t,1)=0,t∈(0,T),σ⁡(T,x)=σT​(x),x∈(0,1),\begin{cases}-\sigma_{t}+\gamma_{1}\sigma_{xxxx}-\sigma_{xxx}+\gamma_{2}\sigma_{xx}=b\psi+g,&(t,x)\in Q_{T},\\ -\psi_{xx}+c\psi=a\sigma,&(t,x)\in Q_{T},\\ \sigma(t,0)=0,\quad\sigma(t,1)=0,&t\in(0,T),\\ \sigma_{x}(t,0)=0,\quad\sigma_{x}(t,1)=0,&t\in(0,T),\\ \psi(t,0)=0,\quad\psi(t,1)=0,&t\in(0,T),\\ \sigma(T,x)=\sigma_{T}(x),&x\in(0,1),\end{cases}

with given final data σT∈H02​(0,1)\sigma_{T}\in H^{2}_{0}(0,1) and right hand sides g∈L2​(0,T,L2​(0,1))g\in L^{2}(0,T;L^{2}(0,1)).

With these, we have the following proposition.

Proposition 2.1.

For given σT∈H02​(0,1)\sigma_{T}\in H^{2}_{0}(0,1) and g∈L2​(0,T,L2​(0,1))g\in L^{2}(0,T;L^{2}(0,1)) or g∈L1​(0,T,H02​(0,1))g\in L^{1}(0,T;H^{2}_{0}(0,1)), there exists unique solution (σ,ψ)(\sigma,\psi) to (2.4) such that

Proof.

We start the proof with the estimate of the elliptic equation. Multiplying the second equation of (2.4) by ψ\psi, then integrating by parts and considering the homogeneous boundary conditions on ψ\psi, we obtain

∫01ψx2+c​∫01ψ2=a​∫01σ​ψ.\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}\psi_{x}^{2}+c\int_{0}^{1}\psi^{2}=a\int_{0}^{1}\sigma\psi.

Recall the Poincaré inequality with best constant:

(2.7) ∫01|ϕ|2≤1π2​∫01|ϕ′|2,∀ϕ∈H01​(0,1).\int_{0}^{1}|\phi|^{2}\leq\frac{1}{\pi^{2}}\int_{0}^{1}|\phi^{\prime}|^{2},\quad\forall\phi\in H^{1}_{0}(0,1).

Then, using the Cauchy-Schwartz and Young’s inequality together with (2.7), we deduce

‖ψ⁡(t,⋅)‖H01​(0,1)\displaystyle\left\|\psi(t,\cdot)\right\|_{H^{1}_{0}(0,1)} ≤C​‖σ⁡(t,⋅)‖L2​(0,1).\displaystyle\leq C\left\|\sigma(t,\cdot)\right\|_{L^{2}(0,1)}.

Next, multiplying the second equation of (2.4) by ψx​x\psi_{xx} and performing the same business as above, we get the following estimate:

‖ψ⁡(t,⋅)‖H2​(0,1)∩H01​(0,1)2≤C​‖σ⁡(t,⋅)‖L2​(0,1)2, for a.e. t in ​[0,T].\displaystyle\left\|\psi(t,\cdot)\right\|_{H^{2}(0,1)\cap H^{1}_{0}(0,1)}^{2}\leq C\left\|\sigma(t,\cdot)\right\|_{L^{2}(0,1)}^{2},\text{ for a.e. t in }[0,T].

Then, integrating on [0,T][0,T], we have

‖ψ‖L2​(0,T,H2​(0,1)∩H01​(0,1))2≤C​‖σ‖L2​(0,T,L2​(0,1))2.\left\|\psi\right\|_{L^{2}(0,T;H^{2}(0,1)\cap H^{1}_{0}(0,1))}^{2}\leq C\left\|\sigma\right\|_{L^{2}(0,T;L^{2}(0,1))}^{2}.

To obtain the regularity result for σ\sigma, let us make a change of variable from tt to T−tT-t so that the first equation of (2.4) becomes forward in time. Then, testing the equation against σx​x​x​x\sigma_{xxxx}, we get

(2.8) ∫01σt​σx​x​x​x+γ1​∫01|σx​x​x​x|2=∫01(b​ψ+σx​x​x−γ2​σx​x+g)​σx​x​x​x.\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}\sigma_{t}\sigma_{xxxx}+\gamma_{1}\int_{0}^{1}|\sigma_{xxxx}|^{2}=\int_{0}^{1}\left(b\psi+\sigma_{xxx}-\gamma_{2}\sigma_{xx}+g\right)\sigma_{xxxx}.

Performing consecutive integration by parts in the first integral and using the Young’s inequality in the right hand side of (2.8), leads to

dd​t​∫01|σx​x|2+γ1​∫01|σx​x​x​x|2≤ϵ​∫01|σx​x​x​x|2+Cϵ​∫01(|ψ|2+|σx​x​x|2+|σx​x|2+|g|2).\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}\int_{0}^{1}|\sigma_{xx}|^{2}+\gamma_{1}\int_{0}^{1}|\sigma_{xxxx}|^{2}\leq\epsilon\int_{0}^{1}|\sigma_{xxxx}|^{2}+\frac{C}{\epsilon}\int_{0}^{1}\left(|\psi|^{2}+|\sigma_{xxx}|^{2}+|\sigma_{xx}|^{2}+|g|^{2}\right).

Using the estimate of ψ\psi from (2.5b) and choosing ϵ=γ1/2\epsilon=\gamma_{1}/2, we get

(2.9) dd​t​∫01|σx​x|2+γ12​∫01|σx​x​x​x|2≤C​∫01(|σ|2+|σx​x​x|2+|σx​x|2+|g|2).\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}\int_{0}^{1}|\sigma_{xx}|^{2}+\frac{\gamma_{1}}{2}\int_{0}^{1}|\sigma_{xxxx}|^{2}\leq C\int_{0}^{1}\left(|\sigma|^{2}+|\sigma_{xxx}|^{2}+|\sigma_{xx}|^{2}+|g|^{2}\right).

Thanks to the Ehrling’s lemma, we have for ϵ>0\epsilon>0,

∫01|σx​x​x|2≤ϵ​∫01|σx​x​x​x|2+K⁡(ϵ)​∫01|σ|2,\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}|\sigma_{xxx}|^{2}\leq\epsilon\int_{0}^{1}|\sigma_{xxxx}|^{2}+K(\epsilon)\int_{0}^{1}|\sigma|^{2},

and applying this in (2.9) for ϵ>0\epsilon>0 small enough and the Poincaré inequality, we have

Then the Gronwall’s lemma yields to

‖σ‖L∞​(0,T,H02​(0,1))≤C​eC​T​(‖σT‖H02​(0,1)+‖g‖L2​(0,T,L2​(0,1))).\displaystyle\|\sigma\|_{L^{\infty}(0,T;H^{2}_{0}(0,1))}\leq Ce^{CT}\left(\|\sigma_{T}\|_{H^{2}_{0}(0,1)}+\|g\|_{L^{2}(0,T;L^{2}(0,1))}\right).

Next, integrating both sides of the inequality (2.10) with respect to (0,t)(0,t) and taking supremum on the both sides for t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T], we shall obtain the L2​(0,T,H4​(0,1))L^{2}(0,T;H^{4}(0,1)) estimate of σ\sigma and finally from the equation of σ\sigma, we obtain σt∈L2​(0,T,L2​(0,1))\sigma_{t}\in L^{2}(0,T;L^{2}(0,1)). The estimate of σt\sigma_{t} can be obtained using the L∞​(H02)L^{\infty}(H^{2}_{0}) and L2​(H4)L^{2}(H^{4}) estimations of σ\sigma. This ensures that σ∈𝒞0​([0,T],H02​(0,1)).\sigma\in\mathcal{C}^{0}([0,T];H^{2}_{0}(0,1)).

On the other hand, assuming g∈L1​(0,T,H02​(0,1))g\in L^{1}(0,T;H^{2}_{0}(0,1)), one can obtain the estimates (2.6a) and (2.6b). ∎

Next let us give the well-posedness of the linearized system (1.7)–(1.5)–(1.6) and (1.8)–(1.5)–(1.6). We only write the details for the system (1.7)–(1.5)–(1.6). For a second order parabolic-elliptic control problem, similar well-posedness results have been appeared in [30].

Definition 2.2.

Let be u0∈H−2​(0,1)u_{0}\in H^{-2}(0,1) and h∈L2​(0,T,H−2​(0,1))h\in L^{2}(0,T;H^{-2}(0,1)). Then, (u,v)∈[L2​(0,T,L2​(0,1))]2(u,v)\in[L^{2}(0,T;L^{2}(0,1))]^{2} is said to be a solution to the system (1.7)–(1.5)–(1.6) if for any g∈L2​(0,T,L2​(0,1))g\in L^{2}(0,T;L^{2}(0,1)) the following holds:

where (σ,ψ)(\sigma,\psi) is a solution of the adjoint system (2.4) with σT=0\sigma_{T}=0.

Moreover, we have the following result.

Theorem 2.3.

Let u0∈H−2​(0,1)u_{0}\in H^{-2}(0,1) and h∈L2​(0,T,H−2​(0,1)).h\in L^{2}(0,T;H^{-2}(0,1)). Then the system (1.7)–(1.5)–(1.6) has a unique solution (u,v)∈[𝒞0​([0,T],H−2​(0,1))]2∩[L2​(0,T,L2​(0,1))]2(u,v)\in[\mathcal{C}^{0}([0,T];H^{-2}(0,1))]^{2}\cap[L^{2}(0,T;L^{2}(0,1))]^{2} with the following estimate:

(2.12) ‖(u,v)‖[𝒞0​(0,T,H−2​(0,1))]2+‖(u,v)‖[L2​(0,T,L2​(0,1))]2≤C​eC​T​(‖u0‖H−2​(0,1)+‖h‖L2​(0,T,H−2​(0,1))).\left\|(u,v)\right\|_{[\mathcal{C}^{0}(0,T;H^{-2}(0,1))]^{2}}+\left\|(u,v)\right\|_{[L^{2}(0,T;L^{2}(0,1))]^{2}}\leq Ce^{CT}\left(\left\|u_{0}\right\|_{H^{-2}(0,1)}+\left\|h\right\|_{L^{2}(0,T;H^{-2}(0,1))}\right).
Proof.

Let us define a linear map ℒ:L2​(0,T,L2​(0,1))↦ℝ\mathcal{L}:L^{2}(0,T;L^{2}(0,1))\mapsto\mathbb{R} by

ℒ⁡(g)=⟨u0,σ⁡(0,x)⟩H−2​(0,1),H02​(0,1)+⟨h,σ⟩L2​(0,T,H−2​(0,1)),L2​(0,T,H02​(0,1)),\mathcal{L}(g)=\left<{u_{0}},{\sigma(0,x)}\right>_{H^{-2}(0,1),H^{2}_{0}(0,1)}+\left<{h},{\sigma}\right>_{L^{2}(0,T;H^{-2}(0,1)),L^{2}(0,T;H_{0}^{2}(0,1))},

where (σ,ψ)(\sigma,\psi) is the solution of the equation (2.4). Thanks to Proposition 2.1, ℒ\mathcal{L} is a continuous linear functional. Thus, by the Riesz-representation theorem, we have a unique (u,v)∈[L2​(0,T,L2​(0,1))]2(u,v)\in[L^{2}(0,T;L^{2}(0,1))]^{2} such that (2.11) holds.

Next, if we define the map ℒ:L1​(0,T,H02​(0,1))↦ℝ\mathcal{L}:L^{1}(0,T;H^{2}_{0}(0,1))\mapsto\mathbb{R} by (2.13), then using estimate (2.6a), we get the continuity of ℒ\mathcal{L}. This yields that u∈L∞​(0,T,H−2​(0,1))u\in L^{\infty}(0,T;H^{-2}(0,1)) satisfying (2.11) and consequently, v∈L∞​(0,T,H−2​(0,1))v\in L^{\infty}(0,T;H^{-2}(0,1)). Indeed, we have the following estimate

(2.13) ‖(u,v)‖L∞​(0,T,H−2​(0,1)×H−2​(0,1))≤C​eC​T​(‖u0‖H−2​(0,1)+‖h‖L2​(0,T,H−2​(0,1))).\left\|(u,v)\right\|_{L^{\infty}(0,T;H^{-2}(0,1)\times H^{-2}(0,1))}\leq Ce^{CT}\left(\left\|u_{0}\right\|_{H^{-2}(0,1)}+\left\|h\right\|_{L^{2}(0,T;H^{-2}(0,1))}\right).

Using standard density arguments, we get the estimate (2.12). Indeed, first taking the initial data regular enough and using the equation (1.7), it can be shown that ut∈L2​(0,T,H−4​(0,1)).u_{t}\in L^{2}(0,T;H^{-4}(0,1)). Using u∈L2​(0,T,L2​(0,1))u\in L^{2}(0,T;L^{2}(0,1)), by classical regularity result, one can conclude that u∈𝒞0​([0,T],H−2​(0,1)),u\in\mathcal{C}^{0}([0,T];H^{-2}(0,1)), and hence v∈𝒞0​([0,T],H−2​(0,1))v\in\mathcal{C}^{0}([0,T];H^{-2}(0,1)). For the less regular initial data, standard density argument and the estimate (2.13) will give the desired result. Similar arguments can be found in [13, Theorem 2.4]. ∎

Analogous to the previous theorem, one can prove the following result when a control is acting in the elliptic equation.

Theorem 2.4.

Let u0∈H−2​(0,1)u_{0}\in H^{-2}(0,1) and h∈L2​(0,T,H−2​(0,1)).h\in L^{2}(0,T;H^{-2}(0,1)). ‖u‖𝒞0​([0,T],H−2​(0,1))∩L2​(0,T,L2​(0,1))+‖v‖L2​(0,T,L2​(0,1))≤C​eC​T​(‖u0‖H−2​(0,1)+‖h‖L2​(0,T,H−2​(0,1))).\displaystyle\left\|u\right\|_{\mathcal{C}^{0}([0,T];H^{-2}(0,1))\cap L^{2}(0,T;L^{2}(0,1))}+\left\|v\right\|_{L^{2}(0,T;L^{2}(0,1))}\leq Ce^{CT}\left(\left\|u_{0}\right\|_{H^{-2}(0,1)}+\left\|h\right\|_{L^{2}(0,T;H^{-2}(0,1))}\right).

3. Control acting in the KS-KdV equation

This section is devoted to study the controllability of our coupled system when a localized control is exerted in the KS-KdV equation. We start by proving the null-controllability of the associated linearized model and as mentioned earlier, using the source term method and a fixed point argument, we will give the required local null-controllability for the nonlinear system.

3.1. A global Carleman estimate

We shall utilize the Carleman technique to deduce the null-controllability of the linearized system.

To do so, let us define the some useful weight functions. Consider a non-empty open set ω0⊂⊂ω\omega_{0}\subset\subset\omega. There exists a function ν∈𝒞∞​([0,1])\nu\in\mathcal{C}^{\infty}([0,1]) such that

(3.1) {ν⁡(x)>0∀x∈(0,1),ν⁡(0)=ν⁡(1)=0,|ν′​(x)|≥c^>0∀x∈(0,1)∖ω0¯ for some ​c^>0.\displaystyle\begin{cases}\nu(x)>0\qquad\forall x\in(0,1),\ \ \nu(0)=\nu(1)=0,\\ |\nu^{\prime}(x)|\geq\widehat{c}>0\ \ \forall x\in\overline{(0,1)\setminus\omega_{0}}\ \ \text{ for some }\widehat{c}>0.\end{cases}

It is clear that ν′​(0)>0\nu^{\prime}(0)>0 and ν′​(1)<0\nu^{\prime}(1)<0. We refer [25] where the existence of such function has been addressed.

Now, for any constant k>1k>1 and parameter λ>0\lambda>0, we define the weight functions

(3.2) φ⁡(t,x)=e2​λ​k​‖ν‖∞−eλ⁡(k​‖ν‖∞+ν⁡(x))t⁡(T−t),ξ⁡(t,x)=eλ⁡(k​‖ν‖∞+ν⁡(x))t⁡(T−t),∀(t,x)∈QT.\displaystyle\varphi(t,x)=\frac{e^{2\lambda k\|\nu\|_{\infty}}-e^{\lambda\big(k\|\nu\|_{\infty}+\nu(x)\big)}}{t(T-t)},\quad\xi(t,x)=\frac{e^{\lambda\big(k\|\nu\|_{\infty}+\nu(x)\big)}}{t(T-t)},\quad\forall\,(t,x)\in Q_{T}.

We have defined the above weight functions by means of the works [44] and [28]. It is clear that both φ\varphi and ξ\xi are positive functions in QTQ_{T}.

We also define

(3.3) \displaystyle φ^(t)=maxx∈[0,1]φ(t,x),φ∗(t)=minx∈[0,1]φ(t,x),\displaystyle\widehat{\varphi}(t)=\max_{x\in[0,1]}\varphi(t,x),\quad\quad{\varphi}^{*}(t)=\min_{x\in[0,1]}\varphi(t,x),
ξ^(t)=maxx∈[0,1]ξ(t,x),ξ∗(t)=minx∈[0,1]ξ(t,x).\displaystyle\widehat{\xi}(t)=\max_{x\in[0,1]}\xi(t,x),\quad\quad{\xi}^{*}(t)=\min_{x\in[0,1]}\xi(t,x).

Some immediate results associated with the weight functions are the followings.

  • –

    For any l∈ℕ∗l\in\mathbb{N}^{*} and s>0s>0, there exists some C>0C>0 such that

    For any (l,n)∈ℕ∗×ℕ∗(l,n)\in\mathbb{N}^{*}\times\mathbb{N}^{*} and s>0s>0, there exists some C>0C>0 such that

(3.8) {−σt+γ1​σx​x​x​x−σx​x​x+γ2​σx​x=b​ψ,(t,x)∈QT,−ψx​x+c​ψ=a​σ,(t,x)∈QT,σ(t,0)=0,σ(t,1)=0,t∈(0,T),σx(t,0)=0,σx(t,1)=0,t∈(0,T),ψ(t,0)=0,ψ(t,1)=0,t∈(0,T),σ⁡(T,x)=σT​(x),x∈(0,1),\begin{cases}-\sigma_{t}+\gamma_{1}\sigma_{xxxx}-\sigma_{xxx}+\gamma_{2}\sigma_{xx}=b\psi,&(t,x)\in Q_{T},\\ -\psi_{xx}+c\psi=a\sigma,&(t,x)\in Q_{T},\\ \sigma(t,0)=0,\quad\sigma(t,1)=0,&t\in(0,T),\\ \sigma_{x}(t,0)=0,\quad\sigma_{x}(t,1)=0,&t\in(0,T),\\ \psi(t,0)=0,\quad\psi(t,1)=0,&t\in(0,T),\\ \sigma(T,x)=\sigma_{T}(x),&x\in(0,1),\end{cases}

with given final data σT∈H02​(0,1)\sigma_{T}\in H^{2}_{0}(0,1).

Theorem 3.1 (Carleman estimate: control in KS-KdV eq.).

Let the weight functions (φ,ξ)(\varphi,\xi) be given by (3.2). Then, there exist positive constants λ0\lambda_{0}, s0:=μ0​(T+T2)s_{0}:=\mu_{0}(T+T^{2}) for some μ0>0\mu_{0}>0 and CC which depend on γ1\gamma_{1}, γ2\gamma_{2}, aa, bb, cc and the set ω\omega, such that we have the following estimate satisfied by the solution to (3.8),

for all λ≥λ0\lambda\geq\lambda_{0} and s≥s0s\geq s_{0}, where IK​S​(s,λ,σ)I_{KS}(s,\lambda;\sigma) and IE​(s,λ,ψ)I_{E}(s,\lambda;\psi) are introduced in (3.6) and (3.7) respectively and φ∗,φ^,ξ^\varphi^{*},\widehat{\varphi},\,\widehat{\xi} are given in (3.3).

Before going to the proof of the above Carleman inequality, let us write the individual Carleman inequalities for the components σ\sigma and ψ\psi.

Proposition 3.2.

Let the weight functions (φ,ξ)(\varphi,\xi) be given by (3.2). Then, there exist positive constants λ1\lambda_{1}, s1:=μ1​(T+T2)s_{1}:=\mu_{1}(T+T^{2}) for some μ1>0\mu_{1}>0 and CC which depend on γ1,γ2,a,b,c\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2},a,b,c and the set ω0\omega_{0}, such that we have the following estimate satisfied by the solution component σ\sigma of (3.8),

for all λ≥λ1\lambda\geq\lambda_{1} and s≥s1s\geq s_{1}, and IK​S​(s,λ,σ)I_{KS}(s,\lambda;\sigma) is introduced by (3.6).

The proof of above such Carleman estimate is initially established in [44]. We also refer [13] where a similar Carleman estimate has been addressed.

Let us also write the following elliptic Carleman estimate (see for instance [25]) satisfied by ψ\psi.

Proposition 3.3.

Then, there exist positive constants λ2\lambda_{2}, s2:=μ2​(T+T2)s_{2}:=\mu_{2}(T+T^{2}) with some μ2>0\mu_{2}>0 and CC which depend on γ1,γ2,a,b,c\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2},a,b,c and the set ω0\omega_{0}, such that we have the following estimate satisfied by the solution component ψ\psi of (3.8),

(3.11) IE​(s,λ,ψ)≤C​∬QTe−2​s​φ​|σ|2+C​s3​λ4​∫0T∫ω0e−2​s​φ​ξ3​|ψ|2,\displaystyle I_{E}(s,\lambda;\psi)\leq C\iint_{Q_{T}}e^{-2s\varphi}|\sigma|^{2}+Cs^{3}\lambda^{4}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\omega_{0}}e^{-2s\varphi}\xi^{3}|\psi|^{2},

for all λ≥λ2\lambda\geq\lambda_{2} and s≥s2s\geq s_{2}, where IE​(s,λ,ψ)I_{E}(s,\lambda;\psi) is introduced by (3.7).

With help of the above two Carleman estimates (3.10) and (3.11), we are now ready to prove the main Carleman estimate (3.9).

Proof of Theorem 3.1.

3.2. Observability inequality and null-controllability of the linearized model

With the Carleman estimate (3.9), it is difficult to obtain the desired observability inequality with norm of the components σ,ψ\sigma,\psi at x=0x=0 in the left hand side. The reason behind is that the weight function e−2​s​φe^{-2s\varphi} is vanishing near t=0t=0.

To avoid this obstacle, we shall proceed as follows. For given T>0T>0, there is some N∈ℕ∗N\in\mathbb{N}^{*}, such that TN≤1\frac{T}{N}\leq 1. We then consider

Below, we sketch the proof of null-controllability for the corresponding linearized system when a control acts on the KS-KdV equation.

Proof of Theorem 1.3–Item 1.

Once we have the observability inequality (3.36), then by standard duality argument, one can prove the existence of a null-control h∈L2​((0,T)×ω)h\in L^{2}((0,T)\times\omega) (in terms of the adjoint component σ\sigma localized in ω\omega) for the linearized system (1.7)–(1.5)–(1.6). This method is standard and has been applied in several works; see for instance the pioneer works [25] or [22, Section 1.3].

Finally, we mention that the cost of control: C​eC/T​‖u0‖H−2​(0,1)\displaystyle Ce^{C/T}\|u_{0}\|_{H^{-2}(0,1)} is followed from the sharp observability inequality (3.36), where C>0C>0 is independent in TT. ∎

3.3. Null controllability of the nonlinear system: control in KS-KdV equation

In this section, by using the control cost of the linear system, given by Theorem 1.3–Item 1, we shall prove the local null-controllability of our nonlinear model (1.3)–(1.5)–(1.6) for given initial data u0∈H−1​(0,1)u_{0}\in H^{-1}(0,1). The proof will be based on the so-called source term method developed in [39] followed by a Banach fixed point argument.

3.3.3. Proof of Theorem 1.1

Proof.

The proof is followed by the Lemma 3.9 and 3.10. Thanks to those results, we can apply the Banach fixed point argument which ensures the existence of a unique fixed point of the map Λ\Lambda in B⁡(0,R)¯⊂ℱ\overline{B(0,R)}\subset\mathcal{F}. Denote the fixed point by f0∈ℱf_{0}\in\mathcal{F}.

Now, in terms of to Proposition 3.8, with the above f0∈B⁡(0,R)¯f_{0}\in\overline{B(0,R)} and initial data ‖u0‖H−1​(0,1)≤R\|u_{0}\|_{H^{-1}(0,1)}\leq R, there exists a control h∈𝒱h\in\mathcal{V} that satisfies the estimate (3.53). Then, the property limt→T−ρ0​(t)=0\displaystyle\lim_{t\to T^{-}}\rho_{0}(t)=0 forces that

(u⁡(T,x),v⁡(T,x))=(0,0),∀x∈(0,1).\left(u(T,x),v(T,x)\right)=(0,0),\quad\forall\,x\,\in(0,1).

This proves the local null-controllability of the nonlinear system (1.3)–(1.5)–(1.6). ∎

4. Control acting in the elliptic equation

In this section, we study the controllability property of the system (1.4)–(1.5)–(1.6), that is when a control locally acts only in the elliptic equation. As earlier, a suitable Carleman estimate is required to get an observability inequality for the linearized model (1.8)–(1.5)–(1.6).

4.2. Observability inequality and null-controllability of the linearized model

Using the Carleman estimate (4.1), one can prove the following observability inequality.

Proposition 4.2 (Observability inequality: control in elliptic eq.).

There exists a positive constant CC depending on ω\omega, aa, bb, cc, γ1\gamma_{1}, γ2\gamma_{2} and NN but not TT, such that we have the following observability inequality

(4.4) ‖σ⁡(0,⋅)‖H02​(0,1)2+‖ψ⁡(0,⋅)‖H2​(0,1)2≤C​eC/T​∫0T∫ω|ψ|2,\displaystyle\|\sigma(0,\cdot)\|^{2}_{H^{2}_{0}(0,1)}+\|\psi(0,\cdot)\|^{2}_{H^{2}(0,1)}\leq{Ce^{C/T}}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\omega}|\psi|^{2},

where (σ,ψ)(\sigma,\psi) is the solution to the adjoint system (3.8).

Proof.

The proof of above proposition will be done in the same spirit of the proof of Proposition 3.5. We skip the details. ∎

The proof of required controllability result, i.e., Theorem 1.3–Item 2 will be followed by a similar argument as we addressed in Section 3.2.

4.3. Null-controllability of the nonlinear system: proof of Theorem 1.2

To prove the null-controllability of the system (1.4)–(1.5)–(1.6), we will follow the same procedure as described in Section 3.3. We shall omit the details for this case since the computations are similar as of Section 3.3.

In what follows, recall the weight functions ρ0\rho_{0}, ρℱ\rho_{\mathcal{F}} and the spaces ℱ\mathcal{F}, 𝒴\mathcal{Y} from Section 3.3. Then, we consider the following system with a source term f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F},

(4.5) {ut+γ1​ux​x​x​x+ux​x​x+γ2​ux​x=f+a​vin ​QT,−vx​x+c​v=b​u+χω​h,in ​QT,u(t,0)=0,u(t,1)=0,t∈(0,T),ux​(t,0)=0,ux​(t,1)=0t∈(0,T)v⁡(t,0)=0,v⁡(t,1)=0t∈(0,T),u⁡(0,x)=u0​(x),x∈(0,1),\begin{cases}u_{t}+\gamma_{1}u_{xxxx}+u_{xxx}+\gamma_{2}u_{xx}=f+av&\text{in }Q_{T},\\ -v_{xx}+cv=bu+\chi_{\omega}h,&\text{in }Q_{T},\\ u(t,0)=0,\ u(t,1)=0,&t\in(0,T),\\ u_{x}(t,0)=0,\ u_{x}(t,1)=0&t\in(0,T)\\ v(t,0)=0,\ v(t,1)=0&t\in(0,T),\\ u(0,x)=u_{0}(x),&x\in(0,1),\end{cases}

with u0∈H−1​(0,1)u_{0}\in H^{-1}(0,1).

Similar to Proposition 3.8, one can prove the following results.

Proposition 4.3.

Let T>0T>0, u0∈H−1​(0,1)u_{0}\in H^{-1}(0,1) and f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F} be given. We also take any (a,b)∈ℝ2(a,b)\in\mathbb{R}^{2} with a≠0a\neq 0. Then, there exists a linear map

(4.6) [u0,f]∈H−1​(0,1)×ℱ↦[(u,v),h]∈𝒴×𝒱,\displaystyle\left[u_{0},f\right]\in H^{-1}(0,1)\times\mathcal{F}\mapsto\left[(u,v),h\right]\in\mathcal{Y}\times\mathcal{V},

such that [(u,v),h]\left[(u,v),h\right] solves (4.5).

Moreover, we have the following regularity estimate

(4.7) ‖uρ0‖𝒞0​(H−1)∩L2​(H01)∩H1​((H3∩H02)′)+‖vρ0‖L2​(H2∩H01)+‖hρ0‖L2​((0,T)×ω)≤C^1​(‖u0‖H−1​(0,1)+‖fρℱ‖L2​((H3∩H02)′)),\left\|\frac{u}{\rho_{0}}\right\|_{\mathcal{C}^{0}(H^{-1})\cap L^{2}(H^{1}_{0})\cap H^{1}((H^{3}\cap H^{2}_{0})^{\prime})}+\left\|\frac{v}{\rho_{0}}\right\|_{L^{2}(H^{2}\cap H^{1}_{0})}+\left\|\frac{h}{\rho_{0}}\right\|_{L^{2}((0,T)\times\omega)}\\ \leq\widehat{C}_{1}\left(\|u_{0}\|_{H^{-1}(0,1)}+\left\|\frac{f}{\rho_{\mathcal{F}}}\right\|_{L^{2}((H^{3}\cap H^{2}_{0})^{\prime})}\right),

where the constant C^1>0\widehat{C}_{1}>0 does not depend on u0u_{0}, ff or hh.

Thereafter, the Banach fixed point argument will give us the required local null-controllability result of the system (1.4)–(1.5)–(1.6), that is Theorem 1.2. We skip the details here since it can be done in a similar fashion as in the previous case.

5. Conclusions and open questions

Let us briefly recall the whole study of the present article. We have considered a coupled parabolic-elliptic system containing a fourth-order parabolic equation, namely KS-KdV and a second-order elliptic equation. Local distributed null-controllability of the aforementioned model has been proved by means of a localized interior control acting only in one equation where the nonlinearity is u​uxuu_{x}.

In both cases, we have established global Carleman estimate which gives rise to some suitable observability inequality and then the usual duality argument provides the null-controllability for the associated linearized models. To this end, we employed the source term method and Banach fixed point argument to obtain the local-null controllability for the nonlinear systems.

One can think of some other issues which has been studied throughout years for various model. Let us mention some of those which can lead some future research direction.

∙\bullet Boundary null-controllability. In [30], the authors studied the boundary local null-controllability of some nonlinear parabolic-elliptic system by means of a single control force acting at the left end of the Dirichlet boundary of parabolic component. They handled the linear model by using a boundary Carleman estimate and then the local inversion technique has been applied to conclude the nonlinear system.

Coming to the KS equation, it is known that to deal with the boundary controllability with single control force, one needs to put some restriction on the anti-diffusion parameter γ2\gamma_{2}. This issues can be overcome by introducing another control in the dynamics (see [9], [10] for more details). Moreover, in [12], the authors studied the local null-controllability of stabilized KS by means of three boundary controls. In the spirit of these aforementioned works, it will be interesting to consider the system with less number of control:

(5.1) {ut+γ1​ux​x​x​x+ux​x​x+γ2​ux​x+u​ux=a​v, in ​QT,−vx​x+c​v=b​u, in ​QT,u⁡(0,x)=u0​(x), in ​(0,1),\begin{cases}u_{t}+\gamma_{1}u_{xxxx}+u_{xxx}+\gamma_{2}u_{xx}+uu_{x}=av,&\text{ in }Q_{T},\\ -v_{xx}+cv=bu,&\text{ in }Q_{T},\\ u(0,x)=u_{0}(x),&\text{ in }(0,1),\end{cases}

with any of the following boundary control data

(5.2) {u(t,0)=q0(t),u(t,1)=0,t∈(0,T),ux(t,0)=0,ux(t,1)=0,t∈(0,T),v(t,0)=0,v(t,1)=0,t∈(0,T), or ​{u(t,0)=0,u(t,1)=0,t∈(0,T),ux(t,0)=0,ux(t,1)=0,t∈(0,T),v(t,0)=p0(t),v(t,1)=0,t∈(0,T).\begin{cases}u(t,0)=q_{0}(t),\ u(t,1)=0,&t\in(0,T),\\ u_{x}(t,0)=0,\ u_{x}(t,1)=0,&t\in(0,T),\\ v(t,0)=0,\ v(t,1)=0,&t\in(0,T),\end{cases}\quad\text{ or }\ \begin{cases}u(t,0)=0,\ u(t,1)=0,&t\in(0,T),\\ u_{x}(t,0)=0,\ u_{x}(t,1)=0,&t\in(0,T),\\ v(t,0)=p_{0}(t),\ v(t,1)=0,&t\in(0,T).\end{cases}

∙\bullet Null-controllability in 2D setting. Controllability of KS-KdV-elliptic equation in higher dimension (in particular 2D) would be an interesting problem to study. For the case of Chemotaxis model (second-order nonlinear parabolic-elliptic equation) [29], the authors obtained the local null-controllability result in bounded domain Ω⊂ℝN,N≥1\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{N},N\geq 1. For the KS equation, the author in [42] studied the local null-controllability in 2D by means of a boundary control by assuming some conditions on the boundary. Thanks to the recent result [37] concerning the spectral inequality for the bi-Laplace operator, the null-controllability of the following system

(5.3) {ut+Δ2​u=χω​h,(t,x)∈(0,T)×Ω,u=0,∂u∂ν=0,(t,x)∈(0,T)×∂Ω,u⁡(0,x)=u0​(x),x∈Ω,\begin{cases}u_{t}+\Delta^{2}u=\chi_{\omega}h,&(t,x)\in(0,T)\times\Omega,\\ u=0,\ \ \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}=0,&(t,x)\in(0,T)\times\partial\Omega,\\ u(0,x)=u_{0}(x),&x\in\Omega,\end{cases}

can be established. On the light of this discussion, it is reasonable to pose a local controllability problem regarding KS-elliptic model in 2D, for instance:

(5.4) {ut+Δ2​u+ν​Δ​u+12​|∇u|2=v+χω​g,(t,x)∈(0,T)×Ω,−Δ​v+γ​v=δ​u,(t,x)∈(0,T)×Ω,\begin{cases}u_{t}+\Delta^{2}u+\nu\Delta u+\frac{1}{2}\left|\nabla u\right|^{2}=v+\chi_{\omega}g,&(t,x)\in(0,T)\times\Omega,\\ -\Delta v+\gamma v=\delta u,&(t,x)\in(0,T)\times\Omega,\end{cases}

with the boundary and initial conditions as in (5.3).
